name: Regular Expressions
author: Recurse
subject: tools
description: Write and read regex patterns: classes, quantifiers, anchors, groups, backreferences and common traps.

lesson.intro: A regular expression is a small pattern language for finding and transforming text. The same core syntax works in editors, grep, JavaScript, Python and most other languages, so a little practice pays off everywhere you search, validate or clean up text.

sections.title: Literals and metacharacters
sections.body:
Most characters match themselves: the pattern `cat` finds the letters c, a, t in a row, anywhere in the text.

A few characters are metacharacters with special meanings: `. * + ? ^ $ ( ) [ ] { } | \`

- `.` matches any single character except a newline.
- To match a metacharacter literally, escape it with a backslash: `\.` matches a real dot, `\$` a dollar sign, `\+` a plus.

Forgetting to escape is the most common regex bug. `3.14` matches "3.14", but also "3x14" and "3-14", because the dot matches anything.

In JavaScript a regex literal goes between slashes, `/cat/`, with flags after the closing slash: `g` finds all matches, `i` ignores case, and `m` makes `^` and `$` work per line.
sections.code:
/3.14/.test("3x14");      // true: . matches any character
/3\.14/.test("3x14");     // false: \. matches only a dot
/a+b/.test("a+b");        // false: + means "one or more a"
/a\+b/.test("a+b");       // true: \+ is a literal plus
"Cat cat".match(/cat/gi);  // ["Cat", "cat"]

check.question: Which pattern matches the literal text (1)?
check.explanation: Both parentheses are metacharacters, so both need a backslash. (1) is a group that matches just the digit 1, [(1)] matches one character from the set, and \(1) leaves an unmatched ) that is a syntax error.

sections.title: Character classes
sections.body:
Square brackets match one character from a set.

- `[aeiou]` matches one vowel, so `gr[ae]y` matches "gray" and "grey".
- A hyphen makes a range: `[a-z]`, `[0-9]`, `[A-Za-z0-9]`.
- A caret at the start negates the set: `[^0-9]` matches any one character that is not a digit.
- Inside brackets most metacharacters are ordinary, so `[.+]` matches a dot or a plus. Only `]`, `\`, a leading `^` and a `-` between characters need care.

Shorthand classes save typing:

- `\d` a digit, `\w` a word character (letter, digit or underscore; ASCII only in JavaScript), `\s` whitespace such as space, tab or newline.
- The uppercase versions are the opposites: `\D` not a digit, `\W` not a word character, `\S` not whitespace.

A class always matches exactly one character. `[abc]` never matches "ab" as a unit; add a quantifier for more.
sections.code:
pattern          matches             does not match
gr[ae]y          gray, grey          groy
[0-9][0-9]       42, 07              4a
[^aeiou]         b, 7, space         a, e
\d\d\d-\d\d\d\d    555-1234            555-12a4
sections.tip: A hyphen first or last in a class is literal: [-+] matches a minus or a plus.

check.question: How many characters does [abc] match at a time?
check.explanation: A character class is one position in the pattern: it matches a single character from the set. To match several, add a quantifier, as in [abc]+.

sections.title: Quantifiers: greedy and lazy
sections.body: A quantifier says how many times the item before it may repeat: - `*` zero or more, `+` one or more, `?` zero or one (optional). - `{3}` exactly three, `{2,4}` two to four, `{2,}` two or more. A quantifier applies only to the single item right before it: in `ab+` the `+` repeats only the `b`. Use a group to repeat more: `(ab)+`. Quantifiers are greedy by default. They take as much text as they can, then give back only what the rest of the pattern needs. Adding `?` after a quantifier makes it lazy, so it takes as little as possible. On the text `bold`, the greedy `<.+>` matches the whole string: `.+` runs to the end and backs up only to the last `>`. The lazy `<.+?>` stops at the first `>` and matches ``. A negated class that cannot cross the delimiter, `<[^>]+>`, is often clearer than a lazy quantifier.
sections.code: const html = "bold"; html.match(/<.+>/)[0]; // "bold" greedy html.match(/<.+?>/)[0]; // "" lazy html.match(/<[^>]+>/)[0]; // "" negated class

check.question: In the pattern ab+, what does the + repeat?
check.explanation: A quantifier applies to the single item just before it, so ab+ matches ab, abb, abbb and so on. To repeat ab as a pair, write (ab)+.

sections.title: Anchors and word boundaries
sections.body:
Anchors match a position, not a character.

- `^` matches at the start of the string and `$` at the end. With the `m` flag they match at the start and end of each line instead.
- `\b` matches a word boundary: a spot with a word character on one side and a non-word character (or the edge of the string) on the other. `\B` matches anywhere that is not a boundary.

Without anchors, a regex matches anywhere inside the text: `\d{5}` happily finds five digits inside "1234567". For validation, where the whole input must fit, wrap the pattern as `^\d{5}$`.

`\bcat\b` finds "cat" only as a whole word, skipping "concat" and "category". Remember that `^` means something else inside brackets, where it negates the class.
sections.code:
/\d{5}/.test("1234567");     // true: five digits found inside
/^\d{5}$/.test("1234567");   // false: the whole string must be five digits
/^\d{5}$/.test("12345");     // true

"cat concat category".match(/\bcat\b/g);  // ["cat"]

check.question: Which pattern requires the entire string to be exactly yes?
check.explanation: ^ anchors to the start and $ to the end, so nothing may come before or after. Plain yes also matches inside "eyes", \byes matches the start of "yesterday", and [yes] matches a single letter.

sections.title: Groups, alternation and backreferences
sections.body:
Parentheses group part of a pattern so a quantifier or alternation applies to all of it, and they also capture the text they matched.

- `|` means or, and it has the lowest precedence of all: `^cat|dog$` means `^cat` or `dog$`. Put alternatives in a group: `^(cat|dog)$`.
- Groups are numbered from 1 by their opening parenthesis, left to right: in `(\d{3})-(\d{4})` group 1 is the first three digits.
- `(?:...)` groups without capturing, for when you only need the grouping.

Captured text can be reused:

- In a replacement string, `$1` and `$2` insert the groups (JavaScript and many tools; Python uses `\1`).
- Inside the pattern itself, a backreference `\1` must match the same text that group 1 matched. `\b(\w+) \1\b` finds doubled words such as "the the".

In JavaScript, `match` without the `g` flag returns an array: index 0 is the whole match, and index 1 onward are the groups.

check.question: When (\d+)-(\d+) matches "10-20", what is group 2?
check.explanation: Groups are numbered by their opening parenthesis from left to right, so group 1 is 10 and group 2 is 20. The whole match, 10-20, is group 0.

keyTerms.definition: A character with special meaning in a pattern, such as . * + ? ^ $ ( ) [ ] { } | or \; escape it with \ to match it literally.
A set in square brackets, such as [a-z] or [^0-9], that matches exactly one character.
A suffix such as *, +, ? or {2,4} that sets how many times the previous item may repeat.
Greedy quantifiers take as much text as possible; adding ? makes them lazy, taking as little as possible.
A zero-width token such as ^ or $ that matches a position, like the start or end of the string.
\b, the position between a word character and a non-word character or the edge of the string.
A parenthesized part of a pattern whose matched text is saved and numbered from 1.
\1, \2 and so on inside a pattern, which must match the same text an earlier group captured.

summary: Escape metacharacters with a backslash when you mean them literally; an unescaped . matches any character.
A character class matches exactly one character from a set; [^...] negates it, and \d, \w and \s are shorthands.
Quantifiers apply to the item just before them and are greedy; add ? for lazy matching or use a negated class.
Anchor validation patterns with ^ and $, and use \b to match whole words.
Group alternatives in parentheses, and reuse captured text with $1 in replacements or \1 inside the pattern.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who has never seen a regex why <.+> matches too much on "bold", and describe two different ways to fix it.

questions.question: Which string does the pattern a.c NOT match?
questions.explanation: The dot must match exactly one character, and it can be any character except a newline: a letter, a real dot or a space. In "ac" there is nothing between a and c, so there is no match.

questions.question: Write a pattern that matches the text 3.14 but not 3x14 or 3-14.
questions.explanation: Escaping the dot with a backslash makes it match only a literal dot. Unescaped, 3.14 also matches 3x14 because . matches any character. 3[.]14 works too, since a dot inside brackets is literal.

questions.question: This should find prices like $25, but it never matches anything. Why?
choices: $ is the end-of-string anchor; escape it as \$ to match a dollar sign
The regex needs the g flag to search past the start of the string
test only checks the beginning of the string
questions.explanation: Unescaped, $ means the end of the input, and no digits can come after the end, so the pattern can never match. /\$\d+/ treats $ as an ordinary character. The g flag is not needed: without it the regex still searches the whole string and stops at the first match.

questions.question: What does [^0-9] match?
choices: Any single character that is not a digit
A digit at the start of the string
questions.explanation: A caret right after the opening bracket negates the class, so it matches one character that is not 0 through 9. It is still a single character, not a run, and ^ means start of string only outside brackets.

questions.question: What does this log?
questions.explanation: \d matches a single digit, and the g flag returns every match, so each of the six digits is its own match. With \d+ the runs would be grouped into 3 matches: "1", "22" and "333".

questions.question: Complete the pattern so it accepts strings made only of hexadecimal digits in either case, such as c0ffee or FF00AA.
questions.explanation: Several ranges can sit side by side in one class: 0-9, a-f and A-F. 0-F is a single range by character code, which also includes : ; < = > ? @ and misses lowercase letters. A comma inside brackets is literal, so 0-9,a-f would accept "1,2" and reject uppercase.

questions.question: What do \d, \w and \s match, and what do their uppercase versions match?
questions.answer: \d matches a digit, \w a word character (letter, digit or underscore), and \s a whitespace character. \D, \W and \S each match any single character that is not in the matching lowercase set.
questions.explanation: These shorthands are character classes, so each matches exactly one character. \d is the same as [0-9], and \D is the same as [^0-9].

questions.question: What does this expression return?
questions.explanation: .* is greedy: it runs to the end of the string, then backs up only until a closing " can match, which is the last quote in the string. So the match runs from the first quote to the last one, not just around "hi".

questions.question: What is the full match? Include the quote characters.
questions.explanation: *? is lazy: it takes as few characters as possible, so the match ends at the first closing quote. The negated class "[^"]*" gives the same result without relying on laziness.

questions.question: Which pattern matches both "color" and "colour" but not "colouur"?
questions.explanation: ? makes the u optional: zero or one. * allows any number, so it also matches colouur; + needs at least one u, so it misses color; and col.r allows exactly one character between l and r, so it misses colour.

questions.question: A PIN must be exactly 4 digits, but this check accepts "12345" and "PIN1234". What is the fix?
choices: Write \d{4,4} so the count is exact
Add the g flag so the whole string is checked
Anchor it as /^\d{4}$/ so nothing can come before or after
questions.explanation: Without anchors, test succeeds if four digits appear anywhere in the input. ^ and $ force the whole string to be exactly those four digits. {4,4} means the same as {4}, the g flag only affects finding multiple matches, and \d never matches letters.

questions.question: What does this expression return?
questions.explanation: \b only requires a boundary before the a. "art" and the start of "artist" both qualify, but in "party" the a follows p, a word character, so there is no boundary there. A second \b after art would leave only the whole word.

questions.question: Complete the pattern so only the standalone word "is" is replaced, giving "this was it".
questions.explanation: \b on both sides requires is to be a whole word, so the is inside "this" is skipped. Plain is replaces both ("thwas was it"), ^is$ needs the entire string to be is, and \sis\s also replaces the spaces ("thiswasit").

questions.question: Which string does ^cat|dog$ match that ^(cat|dog)$ does not?
questions.explanation: | has the lowest precedence, so ^cat|dog$ means "starts with cat" or "ends with dog", and catapult starts with cat. The grouped version requires the whole string to be exactly cat or dog. dogma matches neither: it does not start with cat or end with dog.

questions.question: What string does this return?
questions.explanation: The three groups capture 2024, 06 and 15 in order. The replacement inserts them as $3/$2/$1, which reverses the order and swaps the dashes for slashes.

questions.question: Complete the pattern so it matches a word in matching quotes, like 'hi' or "hi", but rejects mixed quotes like 'hi".
questions.explanation: \1 is a backreference: it must match the same text group 1 captured, so the closing quote has to repeat the opening one. ['"] or a new group accepts either quote, so 'hi" would pass, and $1 is replacement-string syntax that means end of string followed by 1 inside a pattern.

questions.question: What does this log?
questions.explanation: (?:...) groups without capturing, so the (\d+) after the dot is group 1, and it matched 15. If the first group captured, m[1] would be "2".
